title: Signature Events
text:
The Department of Mathematics hosts recurring events that bring together students, alumni, faculty, and guests around mathematics, careers, research, and experiential learning.


Kenneth C. Schraut Memorial Lecture
The Kenneth C. Schraut Memorial Lecture is an annual invited lecture that brings distinguished speakers to the University of Dayton to share ideas and perspectives from across the mathematical sciences.
Held annually


Biennial Alumni Career Seminar
Since 1964, the Biennial Alumni Career Seminar has connected students interested in mathematics with University of Dayton alumni. The seminar helps students explore the breadth of career paths available to those with training in the mathematical sciences and learn how alumni use mathematics in their professional lives.
Held in even-numbered years


Undergraduate Mathematics Day
Undergraduate Mathematics Day brings together students, faculty, and alumni to celebrate undergraduate mathematics. The event provides opportunities for students to share mathematical work, engage in mathematical activities, and connect with the department community.
Held in odd-numbered years


Dayton Data Challenge
The Dayton Data Challenge is a week-long undergraduate data competition in which teams work with real-world data, develop their own questions, use analytical tools of their choice, and communicate their findings.
Visit the Dayton Data Challenge website



#This page is designed as a long-term home for the Department of Mathematics' recurring events. Additional history, photographs, and links to past programs will be added over time.

title: 2026 Events
text:
26th Kenneth C. Schraut Memorial Lecture


Speaker photo
High-resolution publicity photo requested.
Recommended display ratio: 4:5.


Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel
Duke University

Beyond the Prompt: Programming as a Pathway to Statistical Thinking




Abstract
AI tools can now generate polished visualizations, scaffold Quarto reports, and debug data pipelines in seconds. So should statistics and data science students still learn to do these things themselves? The case for teaching programming and reproducible workflows is stronger than ever. When AI can produce code freely, mastery means being able to assess whether that code is correct, recognize when an analysis quietly goes wrong, and structure work so every step can be followed and verified. More importantly, learning modern data science workflows teaches students to think with data: to ask sharper questions, understand what data can and cannot answer, and reason rigorously about uncertainty and statistical models. The code is how we practice these habits; reproducibility is a cornerstone of scientific integrity and an essential skill for working productively with AI. Drawing on experience designing introductory data science courses and curricula, this talk reframes programming instruction in the AI era as a pathway to statistical thinking rather than syntax acquisition. Through concrete examples and ideas for assignments and assessments, it considers how to reward genuine understanding when a plausible-looking answer is only a prompt away. The goal is not to keep AI out of the classroom, but to prepare graduates to critically evaluate what it produces.
